utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. First of all, pursuant to what we said yesterday, we would, indeed, request that we be able to discuss this important issue tomorrow, the issue that was raised yesterday. This morning we have a witness. The first witness will be testifying in closed session with a pseudonym, if the Defence has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Although the issue of law is very important, I think it is best that we decide tomorrow whether we should finish our discussion on that issue or whether we should finish first with the testimony of the witnesses, because it would not be appropriate not to finish with the testimony of the second witness. Let's make that subordinate to the termination of the testimony of the second witness. Otherwise, the witness will be required to remain here during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe we will have any problems finishing, perhaps, even this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, witness, how are you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I want to inform you that you have been granted the protective measures that you have requested, and that you will be referred to as Witness L, and that your face is to be blocked so it cannot be viewed outside this courtroom. And so you may feel comfortable in providing testimony to the Tribunal today. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If there comes a point in the examination where you are required to testify to anything that might identify you, then we will ask the Tribunal to go into closed session, which would mean that your voice would not leave this courtroom, so that you could then feel free to continue that part of your testimony. Is that clear to you and do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: To begin, could you tell us how old you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us whether you have lived in Ahmici, and if so, what year you arrived in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In '74, in '74.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And did you live in Ahmici from 1974 until April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: During that period of time did you live in the same house or did you move from house to house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What part of the village of Ahmici did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sadni Grabovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you tell us who some of your Muslim neighbours were in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sakib Ahmic, Meho, Redzib Ahmic, Suad Zuda, Vehbija, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have any neighbours who were Bosnian Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Who were some of your close Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic, closest neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And before we proceed, could you tell us where you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I live in Ahmici again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When did you move back to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And where in Ahmici did you move back to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a summer house, a summer kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And is this summer kitchen near your former house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe how close the summer kitchen is to your former house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So would it be true to say that the neighbours you had in 1993 are the neighbours you have now? Let me rephrase that question. The Croatian neighbours you had in 1993 are the Croatian neighbours you have now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, before the incident and the attack in 1993, could you describe the kind of relations that you had with your Croatian neighbours, including Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you give us some examples of the kinds of relations that you had with, for example, the Kupreskic family in the years before the attack in '93?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter didn't catch the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer, Witness L, so that the interpreter can hear it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Kupreskic and Gordana were the best man and maid of honour at my wedding, so we have good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to April 15, 1993. That would be the day before the attack. Do you remember what you were doing during that day and where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And where is Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zume is further away from Santici. There is a path there. I mean, it all belongs to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What were you doing in Zume on April 15, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was digging a septic tank, so I was digging, working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And were you doing that most of the day that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had been working for two days and that was the third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And on that day, after you were finished for that day, that is April 15, did you return home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea about when that was when you returned home that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was around 5.00 or 6.00 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was the sun still up or had the sun set at the time that you left to go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it was pretty dark. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, there is a blow-up map behind you. If you could, without standing up, turn around in your seat, if you can, and take a look at that map behind you and see if you can recognise what that shows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse. This is my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let me see if I can orient you a little bit. Do you see where you were working on April 15, 1993 in Zume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see that some Defence counsel can't see the picture, so I wonder whether I could ask the usher to move it a little bit so they can see the whole picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over here, here. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And I know this may be difficult for you, not being used to looking at these aerial photographs. And if it's hard for you, please say so. Is it possible for you to show us on that aerial photograph, if you can, the route you took as you walked home that night on April 15. And if you can't, just simply say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a small path that goes the other way around the stadium from here. There is a stadium and a meadow, and Stipan's house which is next to Vlatko's house. That is the shortest road to Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I notice, as a landmark, you're pointing to a white area on the map which is located towards the right-hand side of that map, for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you see another large white area on the map, located more towards the middle of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You can use your pointer, yes. Does that help you orient yourself in any way on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What is that white area that you've pointed to in the middle of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And do you know who lived in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly Muslims lived there. Croats were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And was your house located in that general area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time I would ask the usher to show the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And perhaps at this time, Mr. President, it would be appropriate to go into closed session because of the house identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look at that photograph, which is marked Exhibit 33, and see if you can recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the big warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is that the warehouse that you walked in front of on April 15, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, if you could use your pointer that's in front of you, take that in your hand, and point to the picture on the table, rather than the picture on the TV screen, and show us where Vlatko Kupreskic was as you walked past on that evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a bench here, and they were sitting there (indicating). The big door was there. This little house was not there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness L, it would be very helpful to the Tribunal if you could actually point to the picture on the table next to you, rather than to the TV screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was where the bench was (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If you could take a green marker, again, I would ask the usher to assist, and place a circle, a red marker would be fine, and place a circle where you recall seeing Vlatko Kupreskic when you passed by on April 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness L, where were you when you saw Vlatko Kupreskic, if you could show us in that photograph, again, using your pointer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I passed by on my way home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Does that photograph show an area where you were standing or walking as you saw Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just right by that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you use your pointer to show us where you were in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Again, if the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating). There, up towards Upper Ahmici, Gornji Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, then, you're pointing to that paved area in front of the shop; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the road to Ahmici leads, up, and there was a parking lot there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were some men also in the area. Where were they when you passed by the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were inside, inside in the warehouse. The doors were always open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, next to this warehouse, there seems to be a newer or another structure attached to that. This would be on the extreme right of the picture. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's bigger now. It was made after, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is this, then, an extension or an addition to the original shop that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, yes, it's an extension along with the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was that extension there in 1993 when you walked past the shop that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would also, at this time, ask that the witness be shown previously admitted Prosecution Exhibit 32.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Vlatko's house, the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that you saw some soldiers in Vlatko's house. Could you, again, use your pointer and, with the assistance of the usher, demonstrate to us where in or around Vlatko's house you saw those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up on the first balcony. Here, on the balcony, the first balcony (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That would be the lower balcony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then proceed on home that evening, on April 15th, to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did you do that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went home and went to bed until 12.00 and had my guard shift afterwards until 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you mean by "my guard shift"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were village guards patrolling the village, village watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, assist in patrolling the village that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from 12.00 to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have any arms with you or weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had my own pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you alone or did you have a partner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A refugee was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was he armed or was he unarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were civilians. No. In fact, we were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone what you had seen earlier that evening, the soldiers in Vlatko's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told Ivo Berberica that there was a sort of army, but that wasn't my affair. That was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What response did you get from the person that you informed? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said that it wasn't my affair and that there was the command and that it was their affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see anything unusual during the two hours that you were walking around the village on the evening of the 15th and the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't see anything strange. We didn't think there was any danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you recall now on the morning of April 16, 1993? If you need to refer to any names of family members -- let me put it this way. You do not need to refer to any names of family members. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. The road went to Sukrija Ahmic's. There was a detonation, gunfire, and they said that a bomb would be thrown, to leave the house. Then Sukrija was killed first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see that. A neighbour of mine, a woman, saw it. We went out of the window, not the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that is out of the window of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In which direction did you run or go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did something happen to you as you ran towards Upper Ahmici from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was wounded in my left arm by Suheta's (phoen) house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't catch that last part of the testimony. You were wounded in your left arm. Then what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A neighbour bandaged it up for me, a woman, and we continued on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you separated from the rest of your family during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. They were in Nermin's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you go after you were injured? Where did you run to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the village of Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you become reunited with your family at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at Vrhovine in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were they okay? Were they all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was burnt down, as well as Mina Sukrija's, Redzep's, and Sesko's. I saw that straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When did you see those houses burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went up the hill, they started to burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you say "they started to burn," who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of those Croats on the day of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where the firing was coming from that injured you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From below Adem Ahmic's house on the left-hand side, and Redzib Ahmic, whichever you prefer to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: After you became reunited with your family, where did you then go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you receive treatment for your injuries in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had an x-ray. I was given injections. I was given some tablets in the hospital on three occasions, and then I had to do some exercises in Zenica, rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, we've talked briefly about Vlatko Kupreskic and your seeing him in front of the shop that day on the 15th. How long had you known Vlatko Kupreskic before that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Since you moved into Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How often had you seen Vlatko Kupreskic during that period of time, from '74 to '93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day, every single day. I always used to pass by there. Just when we were at work we didn't see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you and Vlatko have good relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. With all the Croats we had good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, in 1974, I take it Vlatko was still a fairly young person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He went to third and fourth class at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You were there? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my house is close by. I knew the family, Branka, Vlatko, and Jadranka, all of them. Branka, I think, is the oldest, the daughter. He is an only son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you aware that Vlatko Kupreskic had an operation when he was a child, on his heart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He went to the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: During the period of time that you saw him, almost on a daily basis since he was a child, did you notice whether or not he had any physical problems resulting from either that operation or any other medical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. While he went to school, he didn't have any health problems. He was healthy after the operation, just like other children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: As he grew up to be a young man, did you notice whether he had any physical problems at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He went to the economic school, school of economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Mr. President? I have no more questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moskowitz. Counsel Pavkovic, the usual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you intend to make a pause now, I would like to ask you to do so, actually, so that Defence counsel can discuss the matter of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Actually, we intended to take a break at 12.00, but I understand that it's better for you to break now for 20 minutes? Is that sufficient, 20 minutes? All right, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. I neglected to tender enter into evidence the two exhibits, Exhibit 176, which we request to be under seal, and then 177. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can inform you that the witness will be questioned by counsel Borislav Krajina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try and use up as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Witness L, would you please tell me whether you see in this courtroom Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Where is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right. He has a tie, and is sitting on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked today about the health of Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you whether you had any health problems in your life so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Were you ever treated anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: In no medical institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1991 I had a car -- I had an accident and I was in hospital for 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What kind of accident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Turbe. The accident was in Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had injuries on my left leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you have any other injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was just wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: But not on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No other injuries on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I asked you that because I heard that you had some health problems of a different nature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was hot when I had a bath and I was a little ill but it was nothing dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Where did you have a bath? Where were you -- did you go for treatment anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You didn't go to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, I went to Vitez. It was a lady doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes. And what did she prescribe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She didn't prescribe anything. She just said that I should relax my legs a little bit and that there was no danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: How long did you spend with this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just went that one day. I went back home, and I went back to work afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: And you didn't go to a doctor after that ever again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, what day it was and what time it was on the day that you passed through by the shop of Vlatko Kupreskic and when you saw him there as you described to us today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 5.00 or 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What day was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what day it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You don't know the day. Very well. What was the weather like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Nice weather, you say. Was visibility good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. You could see a little bit. It was dusk. It was April, you know, and days are short in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell us whether you made statements earlier on that it was around 4.00 p.m. in the afternoon, that you once said that it was 4.00 p.m., and on another occasion you said that it was 7.00 p.m. Just let me finish my question, please, and you can give us your answer. And today you state that it was about 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. I'm just asking you whether you said, earlier on, that it was 4.00 p.m. on one occasion and another occasion that you said it was 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said it was getting dark. I don't know what the exact time was, and it's not essential whether it was 4.00 or 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, you leave that up to us to decide whether it's essential or not. I'm just asking you whether you said on two occasions once that it was at 4.00 p.m. and one that it was 7.00 p.m. You just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You did say that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I don't know whether this is a difficult question for you, but I would like to ask you whether you know what the time is now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quarter to twelve. It's noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Noon, you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, thank you. The next thing I want you to tell us who sat with Vlatko Kupreskic at the moment you appeared from work and saw him in front of the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic, Ivica, and Emir Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that in the transcript it does not say that the witness said that Mirko Vidovic was there. It says "Emir". It was Mirko Vidovic, for the transcript. Mirko Vidovic. Thank you. Would you clarify the situation a little bit and tell us where those individuals were, the individuals that you mentioned were with Vlatko sitting in front of the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Were they all in front of the hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Some were inside, but I don't know who these were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Who was inside, who was outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who was inside, but three people were outside and two people that I didn't know. There were five of them outside. Two of them I didn't know. There were five outside, two were unknown to me. The three are -- I knew, and inside --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: How many people were inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten. There were about ten people inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us how you managed to count them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is why I said approximately. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, were they in the hall? Did you go into the hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you can see from outside. There is a big door which is always open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What were they doing inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking. They were discussing something. They were drinking something, talking generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you. Would you please tell us whether, in your previous statements, the statements that you made earlier on, did you state that everything that happened in front of the shop that you saw this in front of Vlatko's house? Did you say in front of house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in front of Vlatko's shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I'm asking you, in your previous statements did you state that all this happened in front of his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, you didn't. Thank you. Will you tell us once again, clearly, whether you drank beer with those individuals and with Vlatko in front of the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In Zume I had three cognacs where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When did you drink cognac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my way home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Three cognacs. How big were those cognacs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know the small glasses. Well, three small glasses of cognac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Do you usually drink alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes. Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Were you ever a drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I was a young man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When was that when you were younger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I was 25, 30. And I don't mind a drop or two even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, that's all right then. Could you tell us whether, in your previous statements, you stated that in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house you drank with him and with the individuals who were in front of the house, whether you drank beer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I just have a little bit longer. I don't want to tire you too much. You said today that you saw, on the balcony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: -- on the first floor--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: -- of Vlatko Kupreskic's house, on the occasion when you were going home from work --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: -- about 30 individuals --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: -- on the balcony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What did these people look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had black and white uniform, military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Black?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: How did you notice that it was a summer uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are summer uniforms and winter uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What do winter uniforms look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're thicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, thicker. You saw this from the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the road is not very far from his house, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Well, can you differentiate whether somebody is wearing a thicker uniform or a lighter uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can quite clearly. Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: You can? Very well then. I apologise for having to ask you the following question, but could you please tell me, looking round the courtroom here, how many people there are? Just look around you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 25 to 30 I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Twenty-five to thirty. Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender in evidence the statement of this witness of the 2nd of February, 1995; and the written notes of the Prosecutor on his talks with this witness, dated the 4th of August, 1998. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution. It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D/13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to make an objection in the sense that this statement be taken into account in the part in which it refers to Vlatko Kupreskic because, otherwise, it makes mention of other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution feels that if the statement is going to be admitted, it should be admitted into its entirety, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But on the other hand -- it is true, but Counsel Puliselic is stating that there is one part of that statement relating to the accused Dragan Papic, and if it is admitted into evidence -- and there was no examination-in-chief on that particular part. I think it's quite sensible to admit this document into evidence, except for the part relating to -- only for the part relating to Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And I think we feel the Court is fully capable of making those distinctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will not take into account any part which does not relate -- any part which relates to people other than Vlatko Kupreskic. So your request, Counsel Puliselic, has been upheld. Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So there is no objection to the witness being released? Witness L, thank you for giving evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, I see that we are short of witnesses, and the -- not even for tomorrow. So can we think of, in future, of having a list of witnesses plus, say, one or two reserve witnesses as it were, so that we don't run out of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think that is a very good suggestion. And we try to do that, and sometimes times we simply do not anticipate accurately how quickly things can move, and perhaps this is a good sign for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, before we adjourn, let me discuss one or two points with you -- raise one or two points. First of all, we have -- now, we are doing some planning, and we understand that it is most likely that the Prosecution will close their case by the 16th of October. Probably even earlier, as we hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We anticipate so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, not after the 16th of October. Now, you may remember that we have now a new Rule, Rule 73 ter, on pre-Defence conference, stating that prior to the commencement by the Defence of its case, the Trial Chamber may hold a conference, and we intend to hold that conference, this pre-Defence conference, and that conference, the Trial Chamber may order that the Defence file the following, and there are various things, submissions by the parties of matters which are not in dispute, statement of contested matters, effect and law, and list of witnesses. So we intend to hold this conference the very same day when the Prosecution finish their case, but we would be very happy if that, say, on the 15th or 16th of October, if at that stage you could already come with a list of witnesses, so that -- and then at that stage we would have a rough idea of how many days, working days, you need, and then later on you will provide, within the time limit we will establish, the summary of the facts. We have already a list of witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic, 20, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, wonderful. Even better. Ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we did not understand each other. We gave this number of witnesses. They are, for the most part, Muslims, which we considered at the time there was the fear that contacting them -- that doesn't mean that -- we do have more witnesses in addition to those that we already mentioned, because those are only the ones that we considered ought to be protected in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I was corrected by my colleagues, there's a list of ten witnesses. I was wrong in saying 20. Ten, plus probably other witnesses. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems, by the reactions of my colleagues, that we could not comply with that request first, because by the 16th we shall be still here. We shall be here. Second, we're going to call the witnesses for which we consider that they should be called after the Prosecutor completes his part of the business, and we'll probably give up calling some witnesses if we consider them -- that it would be superfluous to bring them here, and we if don't wish to go against the Prosecution's assertions. After we complete this part of the hearing, we will have to go and see who we're going to bring, which witnesses we're going to bring. Our list will necessarily, therefore, have to be revised, and for that reason, objectively speaking, we're not going to be able to comply with this request if it were posed in such a way. So we're going to ask to be given some time, and bearing in mind your requests to speed up proceedings and to be as efficient as possible, and we'll be informing you forthwith about the list of witnesses. I think I share the opinions of my colleagues when I say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do appreciate your points, but we were thinking of a tentative list which would not be binding, a rough list, say, 50 or 70 or 80 or 120, just to give us a rough idea and to do some planning, because we have other cases to deal with. As I say, then you may drop some witnesses. You may not even give us the list of names, but I think it would be helpful. But if you are not in a position to give us even a rough list, all right, then we will do without that. In any case, we intend to hold this pre-Defence conference, as I say, when the Prosecution finishes their case. This was one point. The second point is that we are making plans, hoping that security will be provided, to go to Bosnia to visit Ahmici. We would like to go there on Monday, the 19th of October, so as soon as the Prosecution case is over. We understand that we would probably need three days. I understand, also, for budgetary reasons, the Tribunal would cover -- Chambers would cover all the expenses of the Judges, and probably the Prosecution should see whether they can find money. Probably the registry will cover the expenses of Defence counsel, but I assume that not all Defence counsel need to be there. It is important that some of them be there so that we may make sure that both parties are present while we visit the village. Again, make plans so that around the 19th, 20th of October, we'll go there for one day, one full day, plus, of course, travel. Since Defence counsel insist on having four weeks, I've forgotten my diary, but I think we could start on the 23rd -- have you got your diary? It's a Monday, around the 20th of November. Actually, I realise that if we go on until the 18th of December when we intend to finish, Defence counsel would have four weeks. So we are wondering whether the Defence could see whether four weeks would be sufficient, because ideally -- we don't want to force you. Ideally, we could also close the Defence case before Christmas, and maybe if we need time, we might then in January have the closing statements, the final submissions of both parties. This, again, is in the interests of the accused, of a speedy trial. As I say, this is simply to make some plans, not to force the parties to rush. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that you have planned all of that very nicely to end the trial as soon as possible. However, I have to inform you that we are going to tender an expert opinion with the registry and with the Prosecution, too. I imagine that the Prosecutor is going to protest strongly. Of course, if the other side opposes something that an expert witness says, and this expert opinion has to be provided at least 30 days earlier before it is presented as testimony, I'm afraid that the presence of our experts at this Court is going to change your plans somewhat. I mean, the number of witnesses, we will probably be able to give you a tentative figure on that. But this expertise that we are planning will certainly require the appearance of this expert here in The Hague and to be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, and also we will be examining the expert witness a bit. So you can count on the fact that it won't really be possible to finish by the 18th of December, because we could not finish this expertise before we finally questioned a certain witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So, perhaps, you should count on that too, that we also have some surprises too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, one more question which we should not neglect, by any means. All of us can stay here for a period of up to 30 days, according to the visas we have, so not a single one can stay for longer than 30 days. So that question will have to be settled too. We're going to try to settle this matter while we're still here in The Hague, but it doesn't depend on us, of course, because a stay up to 30 days is what we are allowed in one stretch. It is the 14th, and if nothing changes, we can stay only until the 13th of October. We have to leave the country by the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Well, we will ask the Registrar to take all the necessary measures to ensure that you are allowed to stay on until the 16th of October. It's a Friday. We hope that the Prosecution will be a bit quicker. I don't know whether they are going to produce any surprise, I mean, to come up with surprises. As for the expert witnesses, may I insist that, in any case, Rule 94 bis should be complied with and applied by the Defence, as well as the Prosecution. This Rule 94 bis, testimony of expert witnesses, was drafted precisely to avoid any delay in the proceedings. Of course, I agree with Counsel Radovic, if the other party is not going to accept the expert testimony, then the expert witness must be called and give evidence in court. I wonder whether there are any other matters to be raised? Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was thinking of raising an issue or, rather, presenting a proposal in relation to our trip to Ahmici, the one you've been planning. I think that our opinion, that is to say, my opinion and the opinion of my other colleagues, is that before we go, we submit a brief to the Court as to what we, as the Defence, consider to be particularly noteworthy for the Court. That is to say, what the Judges should particularly pay attention to while they are there, what they should especially look at while they are there, and what they should particularly take note of, which would be in the interest of these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We agree. It would be extremely helpful, and, of course, if the Prosecution could do likewise, so much the better. We already have our own ideas and impressions, but we would welcome briefs from both parties. Tomorrow, we may start a bit later. There's no need to rush and to start at 8.30, so we propose to start at 9.30. We will finish when it is necessary, because then we will have to write the ruling after hearing both parties. As I say, I will start with the Defence counsel, if they want to set out their points, or if they want the Prosecution first to make their points and then respond, that's fine with us. The important thing is that both parties should set out their views, and we can then decide afterwards. Before adjourning, since one of the Prosecutors comes from a civil law country and all Defence counsel come, also, from civil law countries, let me raise one issue with you. I know that, probably, it's merely academic, and I apologise to my colleagues, because I didn't discuss this matter before with them and, indeed, tell them that I would raise this issue. I noticed during the testimony of Witness L that one of the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic, was showing his incredulity, and it was very clear that he didn't agree at all with what the witness was saying about him being there and so on. In our countries, this is a typical case where the accused may be asked by the Defence or by the Court to make a statement so as to controvert immediately what the witness is saying. In my own country where now the common law system has been adopted, we have two different approaches to this matter. The witness who is here can give his testimony under oath only in his own defence and normally at the request of the Defence and, I think, also, at the request of the Court. Then he has to tell the truth, because he has to take an oath. This is what we also have in my own country. In addition, we also have the possibility for the accused to make, what we call, “voluntary statements” where he does not have to take an oath, and he can, at any time, tell the Court what he thinks about, say, the particular testimony. Of course, this is of immense value to the Court, because the Court may immediately compare the two statements, that of the witness and that of the accused. Now, I discussed, in general terms, this matter with my colleagues. Of course, we have particular constraints here because of our system, but we can probably find a way. Of course, I think that with the agreement of the parties, to the extent that we don't infringe on the Statute and our Rules of Procedures and Evidence, we might move forward and even take a path which is closer to the civil law system, take up the best elements of the civil law system. Of course, we would need the agreement of the parties, even of Mr. Moskowitz, who is, of course, sceptical because of his cultural background. Just for your consideration. I think we also have to ponder this matter which is difficult, tricky, and, of course, has implications, but I think we should bear it in mind and see whether we can find some way. Because today, as I say, this was a vivid case, a telling case, where the contribution of an accused might have been of great importance to the conduct of our proceedings. Now, my personal view is that, for instance, the accused, if he gives testimony at the request of the Court, for instance, would not be bound by Rule 90, where it is said that: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question." To my mind, the witness, the accused, if he gives testimony in court, has a basic right not to incriminate himself. Therefore, he has a right to refuse to respond. So I would not apply this Rule 90F in this particular case, but this is my personal view, and we have to discuss this matter. As I say, let us try to see whether we could improve upon our system and make it more efficient and more consonant with the interests of justice. I apologise for this long-winded discussion of procedural matters. I think we can now adjourn, and we will reconvene tomorrow at 9.30, probably for one hour, not more than one hour. Thank you. We will find the list of witnesses, I hope, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 12.17 p.m. to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of September, 1998 at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: Pages 2306 to 2335 redacted - in closed session
